reason: The node title promises siento que, the script never uses it, and the bank has both moods (u30-0037 sorry, u25-0392 and u30-1135 feel); the mood switch is standard grammar and the learner has both forms. Severity is medium rather than high, since this is an omission and not an error.
quote: Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape.
replacement: Later this week you'll add *me da pena que*, *me da rabia que* and *me da miedo que*. Same shape. One trap: *siento que* with the wish form means I'm sorry: *Siento que estés triste.* With the plain verb it means I feel or I sense: *Siento que estás triste.*

reason: Siento que tienes que irte is correct Spanish meaning I feel you have to leave, so the old why misdescribes it. English in this file goes in double quotes, not italics (see the rule's "what happened with"), so I changed the markup and shortened one phrase.
quote: Feelings about someone else call for the *tengas* form, not *tienes*.
replacement: To say you are sorry, use the *tengas* form. *Siento que tienes que irte* means "I feel you have to leave".

reason: A present subjunctive after a past verb is grammatical when the ordered event still lies ahead of the moment of speaking, and it is well documented in Latin America (Carrasco Gutiérrez 1999 and Suñer and Padilla-Rivera 1987, from memory; web search did not surface them). It is a recognition note only, so the production rule is untouched.
quote: Teachers call this reported (indirect) commands: the order moves into the past, so the past subjunctive follows *dijo* or *pidió*.
replacement: Teachers call this reported (indirect) commands: the order moves into the past, so the past subjunctive follows *dijo* or *pidió*. If the order still stands, you will also hear the present: *Me dijo que la llame mañana.*
